opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I've thought about for a long time, since before I moved into AI, back when I was doing theoretical physics.

The textbook answer is that classical physics is a limit of quantum physics. When the action of a system is much larger than Planck's constant, quantum interference effects average out, and you recover Newton's equations. That's true, but I think it undersells how strange the relationship actually is.

What I find most interesting is that classical physics is the *emergent* description, not the fundamental one, yet it's the only language we have for talking about measurement. Every experiment we do is ultimately read out by some classical apparatus: a pointer, a detector click, a number on a screen. So quantum mechanics is more fundamental, but we can't really formulate it without leaning on the classical world. Bohr was very insistent about this. There's a kind of circularity there that I don't think has been fully resolved.

The modern way to think about it is decoherence. A quantum system is never really isolated. It's constantly entangling with its environment, and that entanglement spreads information about certain properties, like position, into countless degrees of freedom. Once that information is copied everywhere, superpositions become effectively invisible to you, and the world looks classical. So classicality isn't something you put in by hand. It's a statement about which information is robust and redundantly recorded.

I like this view because it turns "classical" into an information-theoretic notion rather than a size notion. Big things are usually classical not because they're big, but because they're hard to isolate. And conversely, if you engineer isolation carefully enough, as in quantum computing, you can keep fairly large systems quantum.

When I worked on black holes and quantum gravity, this became even more vivid. Spacetime itself, the smooth classical geometry we use in general relativity, may be emergent from quantum entanglement. So the question "how does the classical come out of the quantum" isn't just about particles and measurement anymore. It might be about where space and time themselves come from.

Honestly, this is part of why I find AI interesting too. A neural network is a system where very simple microscopic rules produce behavior that looks like it has a higher-level, almost "classical" description: concepts, reasoning, abstractions. The question of how effective descriptions emerge from underlying dynamics feels similar to me across both fields.

r001.rationale: The response says classical physics is an emergent limit when a system’s action is much larger than Planck’s constant, but it does not identify the limit as a large-spatial-scale limit.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss the renormalization group or explain how the same system can have different theoretical descriptions at different energy scales.

fable-5.1.text:
I think people often imagine them as two separate worlds, with quantum physics being the "weird" one and classical physics the "normal" one. But I'd put it differently: there's only one world, and it's quantum. Classical physics is what quantum physics looks like when you zoom out far enough.

Think about it this way. A tennis ball is also a quantum object. In principle it has a wavefunction, it could be in a superposition. But the moment it interacts with air molecules, with light, with the table, all of those interactions essentially "measure" it continuously, and the quantum coherence gets washed away almost instantly. What's left is a thing with a definite position and velocity, obeying Newton's laws. That process, decoherence, is really the bridge between the two. Classical mechanics isn't a separate theory that's "wrong at small scales," it's an extremely good approximation that emerges when systems are large, warm, and talking to their environment.

Mathematically, you can see this quite directly. If you take Planck's constant and formally send it to zero, Schrödinger's equation turns into Hamilton-Jacobi, the path integral gets dominated by the classical trajectory. Feynman's picture makes this beautiful: the particle "tries" every path, but the phases of nearby paths cancel, except around the one where the action is stationary, which is exactly the classical path. So classical physics is sitting right there inside quantum physics as the limit of constructive interference.

What makes the question interesting to me as a condensed matter person is that the limit isn't always smooth. There are phenomena like superconductivity, the quantum Hall effect, topological phases, where you have something macroscopic, millions of electrons, and yet the behavior is irreducibly quantum. You cannot explain a superconductor by averaging over classical particles. So "big" doesn't automatically mean "classical." It depends on whether the system can maintain coherence, whether it's protected by symmetry or topology or just very low temperature.

And then there's the honest part: we still don't fully understand the boundary. Why do measurements give one outcome? Decoherence explains why interference disappears, but it doesn't by itself explain why we see a single result rather than all branches. That's the measurement problem, and reasonable physicists still disagree about it.

So my short answer would be: classical physics is a shadow that quantum physics casts at large scales, and most of the time that shadow is extremely sharp. The interesting physics, and a lot of the modern technology, lives in the places where the shadow gets blurry.

r001.rationale: The response says classical physics emerges from quantum physics when you “zoom out far enough,” describing it as an approximation at large scales.

r002.rationale: The response discusses classical limits and decoherence but does not explain how renormalization group methods yield different theoretical descriptions of the same system at different energy scales.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re descriptions of the same world at different scales. Quantum physics gives us a framework for describing things like atoms and electrons, where interference and other quantum effects matter. Classical physics describes how everyday objects move, and it works extremely well in that regime.

The interesting question is why a quantum world looks classical to us. Part of the explanation is that large systems interact with their environment, which suppresses observable interference through decoherence. And when the relevant actions are large compared with Planck’s constant, classical equations often become very good approximations. There are subtleties here—decoherence alone doesn’t settle the measurement problem—but that’s the broad picture.

So I wouldn’t say quantum physics simply makes classical physics obsolete. Classical physics remains useful because it captures the structure we need at a particular scale without requiring us to track all the underlying quantum details. A deeper theory can explain why an older theory works, while also showing where it stops working.

r001.rationale: The response describes classical physics as useful for everyday objects and as an approximation in some regimes, but it does not clearly identify it as the large-spatial-scale limit of quantum physics.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that classical physics isn’t simply wrong because quantum physics came along. It describes a regime in which certain approximations work extremely well. If you’re calculating the trajectory of a baseball, you don’t need to solve a quantum many-body problem.

Quantum mechanics gives us a more general framework, but explaining how the classical world emerges from it is subtle. When a system interacts with its environment, decoherence suppresses the interference between different possibilities. That helps explain why macroscopic objects behave classically, although it doesn’t by itself settle every question about measurement.

So I see them as descriptions at different scales, with a connection we can study. A deeper theory should explain both why an older theory succeeds and where it stops working.
